articles.title: A planet 320 light-years away confirms what scientists long suspected
articles.summary: Astronomers have discovered that a scorching-hot planet 320 light-years away shares a striking chemical similarity with its host star, providing the first direct evidence for a fundamental assumption about planet formation. The breakthrough could help scientists predict what distant rocky planets are made of and identify worlds with conditions favorable for life.
articles.content:
A scorching hot planet nearly 320 light-years from Earth has provided the first direct evidence for a fundamental assumption about how planets form. Astronomers discovered that WASP-189b shares an important chemical characteristic with its host star, supporting a long-standing idea that also helps scientists investigate potentially habitable worlds. The breakthrough came from the first simultaneous measurement of gaseous magnesium and silicon in an exoplanet's atmosphere, using the Gemini South telescope, part of the International Gemini Observatory, which is partially funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation and operated by NSF NOIRLab.

Located nearly 320 light-years away in the Libra constellation, WASP-189b belongs to an extreme category of planets called ultra-hot Jupiters (UHJ). These enormous worlds reach temperatures so intense that even materials normally found in solid rock can turn into gas. Elements such as magnesium (Mg), silicon (Si), and iron (Fe) can therefore be detected in their atmospheres. Astronomers identify these substances through spectroscopy, a method that separates light into different wavelengths to reveal the chemicals present.

An international research team led by Jorge Antonio Sanchez, a graduate student at Arizona State University (ASU), investigated WASP-189b with the high-resolution Immersion GRating INfrared Spectrograph (IGRINS). At the time, the instrument was installed on the Gemini South telescope in Chile.[1]

For the first time, researchers were able to measure magnesium and silicon together in the atmosphere of a planet beyond our Solar System. Their observations revealed that the proportion of magnesium to silicon on WASP-189b closely matches the ratio found in its parent star. This result provides the first direct observational support for a widely used assumption about the chemical relationship between stars and their planets, offering a valuable new way to investigate planetary origins and evolution.

"These discoveries show Gemini's ability to help us understand the characteristics of the remarkable zoo of exoplanets in our solar neighborhood," says Chris Davis, NSF Program Director for NOIRLab. "Such discoveries are only possible because of Gemini's cutting-edge instruments."

A Long-Suspected Connection Between Stars and Planets

Astronomers believe that giant planets such as WASP-189b formed within enormous disks of gas and dust surrounding young stars. These structures, called protoplanetary disks, provide the raw materials from which planets develop. The chemical makeup of a giant planet's outer atmosphere is thought to retain clues about the environment where it originally formed.

Because stars and their surrounding disks originate from the same cloud of material, scientists have long assumed that they contain similar proportions of rock-forming elements. In particular, the ratios of these elements in a disk are expected to resemble those measured in its central star.

This relationship has become an important tool for predicting the composition of rocky exoplanets. Until now, however, the assumption was supported primarily by evidence from our own Solar System. Astronomers had not directly measured the same relationship in a planet orbiting another star.

The discovery involving WASP-189b provides that missing observational evidence, strengthening the scientific basis for using stellar chemistry to understand the materials from which distant planets form.

"WASP-189b gives us a much-needed observational anchor in our understanding of terrestrial planet formation since it offers a measurable quantity that validates the presumed resemblance of stellar composition and the proportion of rocky material around host stars used to form planets," says Sanchez.

What Planetary Chemistry Could Reveal About Habitability

The implications reach beyond understanding how planets are assembled. This chemical relationship is also important in astrobiology, which investigates the possibility of life beyond Earth and the environmental conditions that could support it, including habitable environments within our Solar System.

By studying the elements present in a star, astronomers may be able to estimate the relative amounts of rock-forming materials available to its planets. These materials influence a planet's internal structure, geological activity, and chemical environment, all of which can affect whether conditions suitable for life might develop.

Earth provides a familiar example. The elements that make up our planet help determine processes such as plate tectonics, the generation of its protective magnetic field, and the movement of essential chemicals into the atmosphere, oceans, and soil. Together, these processes contribute to the environment that allows life to thrive.

As researchers work toward studying smaller, rocky exoplanets in greater detail, establishing a reliable connection between stellar chemistry and planetary composition becomes increasingly important. The WASP-189b findings provide a significant step in that direction.

Powerful Telescopes Open a New Window Into Alien Atmospheres

Obtaining these measurements requires instruments capable of distinguishing extremely fine details in the light collected from distant planetary atmospheres. According to the researchers, the necessary spectral resolution for this kind of analysis is currently available only through ground-based telescopes.

"Our study demonstrates the capability of ground-based, high-resolution spectrographs to constrain critical species like magnesium and silicon, which are two elemental building blocks from which rocky planets form," says study co-author Michael Line, Associate Professor at ASU. "This advancing capability opens an entirely new dimension in our study of exoplanet atmospheres."

The team expects future observations using multiple wavelengths and similarly precise instruments to uncover a wider range of elements in exoplanet atmospheres. Building a more complete picture of their chemical compositions could reveal additional clues about how planets form, how they change over time, and which conditions might favor habitability.

By connecting the chemistry of a distant planet to that of its star, astronomers now have new evidence supporting a principle that could help guide the search for potentially habitable worlds throughout the galaxy.

Notes

This discovery has broad implications for understanding planetary origins and assessing habitability of exoplanets, representing a meaningful advancement in space science with potential benefits for astrobiology and the search for life beyond Earth.

articles.title: Voyager Technologies’ Griffin-1 Completes Environmental Testing at NASA JPL
articles.summary: Description A lunar lander from Voyager Technologies completed nearly three months of environmental testing at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California in late September 2026. The tests demonstrate that the spacecraft is prepared to face the harsh conditions of launch, its journey to the Moon, and landing on the surface. Its final trial was […]
articles.content:
Description

A lunar lander from Voyager Technologies completed nearly three months of environmental testing at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California in late September 2026. The tests demonstrate that the spacecraft is prepared to face the harsh conditions of launch, its journey to the Moon, and landing on the surface. Its final trial was in JPL’s historic 25-Foot Space Simulator, a thermal vacuum chamber listed on the National Register of Historic Places for its role in supporting historic missions like those of the Ranger, Surveyor, Mariner, and Voyager programs.

Engineers and technicians on Aug. 31, 2026, used a crane to position the spacecraft within the towering chamber, where Griffin-1 alternately baked at up to 167 degrees Fahrenheit (75 degrees Celsius) and froze at temperatures as low as minus 148 F (minus 100 C). This thermal vacuum testing simulates the extreme temperatures the spacecraft will experience during its mission. The yellow-striped box atop the lander simulates a payload that will later be attached to the spacecraft: Astrolab’s FLIP (FLEX Lunar Innovation Platform) rover.

Figure A

In Figure A, engineers and technicians move Griffin-1 through a hallway leading to the 25-Foot Space Simulator on Aug. 31. The corridor is lined with photographs of some of the historic spacecraft that have been tested in the facility since the 1960s.

Figure B

Figure B shows Griffin-1 on July 29 in an anechoic chamber for electromagnetic interference and electromagnetic compatibility testing, which ensures signals from the spacecraft’s electronic components don’t interfere with one another. Long foam spikes line the chamber walls to absorb sound waves and electromagnetic waves.

Figure C

In Figure C, taken on July 20, Griffin-1 rotates rapidly on a special table to measure its mass properties, enabling engineers to look for any unexpected wobbles as they assess how the vehicle will move through space — vital information for determining the spacecraft’s readiness for flight and surface operations.

Figure D

In Figure D, microphones are arrayed around Griffin-1 on Aug. 12 during acoustic testing in which giant horns powered by compressed gaseous nitrogen blast the spacecraft with up to 153 decibels inside the sealed acoustic chamber to mimic the roar of launch.

Griffin-1 also endured vibration testing, during which hundreds of sensors monitored the spacecraft as a “shaker table” rattled it in three directions — with increasingly intense force — to simulate the ride out of Earth’s atmosphere atop a rocket.

After proving its mettle at JPL, Griffin-1 was shipped back across the country to Voyager Lunar Systems’ Pittsburgh facility for final assembly. Part of NASA’s CLPS (Commercial Lunar Payload Services) initiative within the Moon Base Program, Griffin-1 is expected to launch in late 2026 aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket. The infrastructure-class lander will deliver more than 1,100 pounds (455 kilograms) of cargo — 10 payloads from six countries — to Nobile Crater near the lunar South Pole.

Caltech in Pasadena, California, manages JPL for NASA.

The article provides detailed context about the testing process and the mission's scope, highlighting a meaningful advancement in space technology with potential large-scale benefits for humanity's understanding and presence in space.

articles.title: Perseverance Navcam Image Marks Record Drive
articles.summary: Description Rover tracks and a rocky Martian landscape are shown in this image captured by one of the navigation cameras (navcams) aboard NASA’s Perseverance Mars rover on Oct. 11, 2026, the 2,006th Martian day, or sol, of the mission. During that sol’s drive, spanning 299.6 feet (91.31 meters), the mission passed a major milestone: pushing Perseverance’s total […]
articles.content:
Description

Rover tracks and a rocky Martian landscape are shown in this image captured by one of the navigation cameras (navcams) aboard NASA’s Perseverance Mars rover on Oct. 11, 2026, the 2,006th Martian day, or sol, of the mission. During that sol’s drive, spanning 299.6 feet (91.31 meters), the mission passed a major milestone: pushing Perseverance’s total driving distance beyond that of the agency’s Opportunity rover, which logged 28.06 miles (45.16 kilometers) during its 15-year mission on Mars.

NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, which is managed for the agency by Caltech in Pasadena, California, built and manages operations of the Perseverance rover on behalf of the agency’s Science Mission Directorate in Washington, as part of NASA’s Mars Exploration Program portfolio.

For more about Perseverance: https://science.nasa.gov/mission/mars-2020-perseverance/
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant milestone in space exploration, with NASA's Perseverance rover surpassing the total driving distance of the previous Opportunity rover on Mars. This achievement reflects progress in robotic exploration of Mars, which has broad scientific and inspirational impact for humanity.
articles.personality_title: NASA’s Perseverance rover breaks distance record on Mars
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – NASA’s Perseverance rover has been exploring Mars since 2021. It uses special cameras called navigation cameras, or navcams, to see the terrain as it drives across the rocky surface of the planet.

**What happened** – On October 11, 2026, during its 2,006th day on Mars, Perseverance drove nearly 300 feet (91 meters) in one day. This drive helped the rover pass an important milestone by traveling farther than NASA’s previous rover, Opportunity, which covered about 28 miles (45 kilometers) over 15 years.

**Impact** – This achievement shows how much technology has improved. Perseverance has been able to explore Mars much more quickly and cover greater distances than before. This allows scientists to study more places on Mars and learn more about the planet’s history and conditions.

**What’s next step** – Perseverance will continue its journey across Mars, collecting samples and sending data back to Earth. Its success may also guide future missions, both robotic and eventually human, to explore Mars more efficiently.

**One-sentence takeaway** – NASA’s Perseverance rover has set a new record for the longest distance traveled on Mars, surpassing its predecessor and advancing our exploration of the Red Planet.

articles.title: Dinosaur named new species a century after fossil found on Isle of Wight
articles.summary: Invictibellatrix amberina, a predator in the megaraptoran group of dinosaurs, lived in what is now Britain 120 million years ago and may have had claws 20 centimetres long
articles.content:
Invictibellatrix amberina, a predator in the megaraptoran group of dinosaurs, lived in what is now Britain 120 million years ago and may have had claws 20 centimetres long

An artist’s illustration of the new theropod dinosaur, Invictibellatrix amberina Sergey Krasovskiy and Pedro Salas

Meet Invictibellatrix amberina, the unconquered female warrior – a new species of predatory dinosaur related to Tyrannosaurus rex that hails from the Isle of Wight in southern England.

The fossil used to identify it – a partial braincase – has been lying in the archives of the Natural History Museum in London since it was acquired from a Reverend Reginald Hooley in 1924. “It was sitting unstudied in the museum for about 100 years, which is very surreal,” says Cassius Morrison, now at the University of Leeds, UK.

Morrison and his colleagues used CT scans to create a 3D scan of the fossil and compared it with features of other dinosaurs.

Advertisement

The closest match was the Argentinian megaraptoran Murusraptor from about 80 million years ago. So, the researchers suggest that the skull, originally found in 120-million-year-old rocks from the Lower Cretaceous Wessex Formation on the south-west coast of the Isle of Wight, is from a new species belonging to the Megaraptora group of carnivorous dinosaurs. If so, it is the first time a megaraptoran has been discovered in Europe.

The fossil braincase of Invictibellatrix amberina. The oval hole is where the brain would have been The Trustees of the Natural History Museum, London

A similar-looking dinosaur is known from a few million years earlier in the Wessex Formation: the 5-metre-long Eotyrannus. However, the parts we have hint that it belonged to the sister group of tyrannosaurs and none of the fossilised remains of the two individuals directly overlap, so it is hard to compare them.

The genus name Morrison and his colleagues have given to the newly described fossil, Invictibellatrix, means female unconquered warrior. They estimate that it was an agile, two-legged carnivore that was about 3 to 4 metres long, some 1.5 metres tall and weighing between 200 and 300 kilograms. It is likely to have had feathers and claws 10 to 20 centimetres long for attacking small dinosaurs, lizards and mammals, says Morrison.

Had we been around then, “humans would have been perfect-sized prey, about a third of their body weight,” he says.

At the time, the Isle of Wight was still firmly attached to both mainland Britain and the rest of Europe, and the environment would have been subtropical, says Morrison.

Megaraptoran fossils have been found in Asia, Australia and South America, and finding one in Europe would begin to tie their story together.

Morrison suggests that Invictibellatrix evolved from Asian megaraptorans that dispersed into Europe some 130 million years ago. Then megaraptorans spread from Europe to Africa, then to South America and Australia before the continents completely separated.

Jake Kotevski at Monash University in Melbourne says it is a shame more detailed comparisons couldn’t be made with Eotyrannus, which has previously been considered a relative of megaraptorans.

“If Invictibellatrix is indeed a megaraptoran, it expands the palaeobiogeographic range of the group and plugs a significant gap in our knowledge, linking those from South-East Asia to Australia and South America via Europe and Africa,” he says. “However, more fossils are required to support or reject this hypothesis.”
